title: "Composing Pipelines"

# Composing Pipelines

A pipeline is a sentence: start from a source, keep or change items, finish in one consumer. These recipes are full sentences. The last one is the sentence you should not write.

## The concept

Name an intermediate iterator when a step needs a type the compiler cannot see, or when a `?` has to live in a function rather than a closure. Keep the closure bodies short. A closure that matches five cases is a function, and the call site is often a loop.

## Recipe 29 — Building a log processing pipeline

Each line is `level sensor=value`. Keep `WARN` and `ERROR`, and turn them into owned messages.

```rust
fn main() {
    let raw = "\
INFO sensor=temp value=20
WARN sensor=temp value=81
INFO sensor=fan value=1200
ERROR sensor=disk value=full
";

    let alerts: Vec<String> = raw
        .lines()
        .filter(|line| line.starts_with("WARN") || line.starts_with("ERROR"))
        .map(|line| {
            let mut parts = line.split_whitespace();
            let level = parts.next().unwrap_or("?");
            let rest = parts.collect::<Vec<_>>().join(" ");
            format!("{level}: {rest}")
        })
        .collect();

    assert_eq!(
        alerts,
        ["WARN: sensor=temp value=81", "ERROR: sensor=disk value=full"]
    );
}
```

`lines` borrows `raw`. The `format!` at the end owns the text the caller keeps, so the result does not borrow `raw`.

## Recipe 30 — Parsing a CSV with a fallible pipeline

One bad field fails the whole collect. The row number is the `enumerate` index plus one, with the header on row 1.

```rust
fn main() {
    let csv = "\
name,age
ada,36
linus,nope
grace,40
";

    let parsed = parse_people(csv);
    assert!(parsed.is_err());

    let ok = "\
name,age
ada,36
grace,40
";
    assert_eq!(
        parse_people(ok).unwrap(),
        [Person { name: "ada".into(), age: 36 }, Person { name: "grace".into(), age: 40 }]
    );
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u32,
}

fn parse_people(csv: &str) -> Result<Vec<Person>, String> {
    csv.lines()
        .skip(1)
        .enumerate()
        .map(|(index, line)| {
            let row = index + 2;
            let mut fields = line.split(',');
            let name = fields.next().unwrap_or("").trim();
            let age_text = fields.next().unwrap_or("").trim();
            let age: u32 = age_text
                .parse()
                .map_err(|_| format!("row {row}: age {age_text:?} is not a number"))?;
            if name.is_empty() {
                return Err(format!("row {row}: missing name"));
            }
            Ok(Person { name: name.to_string(), age })
        })
        .collect()
}
```

`collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()` is inferred from the function's return type. It stops allocating the success path at the first `Err` and returns that error. Later rows are not parsed.

The `?` is inside `map`'s closure, and the closure returns `Result`. That is legal. `?` returns from the closure, not from `parse_people`. The `collect` is what turns a sequence of results into one result.

## Recipe 31 — Deduplicating and normalizing a sequence

The standard library has `dedup` on `Vec`, and it only removes neighbors that are equal. Sort first if you want set-like uniqueness and you also want a stable order.

```rust
fn main() {
    let raw = [" Ada ", "ada", "LINUS", "linus", "Ada"];
    let mut names: Vec<String> = raw.iter().map(|text| text.trim().to_lowercase()).collect();
    names.sort();
    names.dedup();
    assert_eq!(names, ["ada", "linus"]);
}
```

Order of first appearance, without a sort, needs a `HashSet` of keys you have already emitted:

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::collections::HashSet;

    let raw = [" Ada ", "LINUS", "ada"];
    let mut seen = HashSet::new();
    let names: Vec<String> = raw
        .iter()
        .map(|text| text.trim().to_lowercase())
        .filter(|name| seen.insert(name.clone()))
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(names, ["ada", "linus"]);
}
```

`HashSet::insert` returns `true` when the key was new. The filter keeps those. This allocates a `String` for the set and moves another into the `Vec`. That is the cost of preserving first-seen order.

## Recipe 32 — Grouping elements with fold() and a HashMap

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::collections::HashMap;

    let names = ["ada", "linus", "grace", "alan"];
    let by_letter = names.iter().fold(HashMap::<char, Vec<&str>>::new(), |mut groups, name| {
        let letter = name.chars().next().unwrap();
        groups.entry(letter).or_default().push(*name);
        groups
    });

    assert_eq!(by_letter.get(&'a'), Some(&vec!["ada", "alan"]));
    assert_eq!(by_letter.get(&'l'), Some(&vec!["linus"]));
}
```

`entry` + `or_default` creates the `Vec` on first sight of a letter. `fold` returns the map. A `for` loop that mutates an outer `HashMap` is the same program and is often easier to read. The fold form is here because the recipe is "grouping without a separate loop variable".

## Recipe 33 — Flattening a pipeline with nested Options and Results

Each `flatten` peels one layer. `Option` and `Result` are iterable.

```rust
fn main() {
    let nested = vec![Some(Some(1)), Some(None), None, Some(Some(2))];
    let values: Vec<i32> = nested.into_iter().flatten().flatten().collect();
    assert_eq!(values, [1, 2]);
}
```

This throws away the distinction between "missing" and "present but empty". For `Result`, it also throws away the error:

```rust
fn main() {
    let rows: Vec<Result<i32, &str>> = vec![Ok(1), Err("bad"), Ok(2)];
    let kept: Vec<i32> = rows.into_iter().flatten().collect();
    assert_eq!(kept, [1, 2]);
}
```

Use that only when the error is intentionally ignored. The error-handling chapter collects the failures instead.

## Recipe 34 — Knowing when not to use a pipeline

This chain updates a counter, records two different failures, and stops early. It is legal Rust. It is a worse program than the loop under it.

```rust
fn main() {
    let rows = ["1", "2", "nope", "4"];

    let mut parsed = Vec::new();
    let mut skipped = 0;
    for (index, row) in rows.iter().enumerate() {
        match row.parse::<i32>() {
            Ok(n) => parsed.push(n),
            Err(_) => {
                skipped += 1;
                if skipped == 1 && index > 0 {
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
    }
    assert_eq!(parsed, [1, 2]);
    assert_eq!(skipped, 1);
}
```

The stop condition mentions both the failure count and the index. Forcing that into `take_while` or `try_fold` hides the rule. The "when not to" chapter lists more of these shapes. The test for this recipe is: can you read the stop rule out loud from the code without drawing it? If not, use the loop.
